section_summaries.epidemiology: Monkeypox virus, first identified in captive monkeys in 1958, is endemic to tropical rainforests of central and western Africa, with most human cases occurring in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Outbreaks have increased, including the first reported outside Africa in 2003 in the midwestern United States, traced to imported African rodents. Humans contract monkeypox through direct contact with infected animals (e.g., great apes, monkeys, pigs, hedgehogs, squirrels, rats) or person-to-person transmission via respiratory droplets, accounting for 10% to 30% of cases. The natural reservoir is unknown but likely involves rope squirrels or other terrestrial rodents. The first human case was in 1970, and active surveillance in the DRC (1981-1986) identified 338 cases with 28% secondary human-to-human transmission. Recent data suggest an increased risk for human-to-human transmission, with a 20-fold increase in incidence in the DRC after smallpox cessation, placing unvaccinated individuals at 5.2-fold increased risk.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Monkeypox infection begins with virus entry into the dermis (from animal contact) or respiratory epithelium (from person-to-person). The virus then disseminates through the lymphatic system, leading to primary and secondary viremia, which results in infection of the epithelium and the production of skin and mucosal lesions. The incubation period is typically 7 to 14 days, and patients are infectious during the first week of rash. Virulence differs between West African and Congo basin isolates, with Congo basin isolates exhibiting more robust replication. Monkeypox viruses evade host immune responses, allowing them to form plaques and replicate within the host cell cytoplasm.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Clinical manifestations of monkeypox typically begin with a prodrome of fever, headache, myalgia, backache, and prominent lymphadenopathy 1 to 5 days before rash onset. Lymphadenopathy (post-auricular, axillary, or inguinal) occurs 1-2 days before the rash, distinguishing it from smallpox. Skin lesions develop concurrently, progressing at a similar rate over 2 to 4 weeks, from small papules (2-5 mm) through vesicular, pustular, and crusted stages over 2 to 3 weeks. The rash is typically more severe on the head and extremities, including palms and soles, and less intense on the trunk. Scabs slough off, leaving depigmented scars. Complications include secondary bacterial infection of skin lesions, pneumonitis, and eye involvement. Death occurs in approximately 10% of cases, usually in the second week of illness. Prior smallpox vaccination with vaccinia virus results in milder disease, fewer skin lesions, less lymphadenopathy, and significantly lower mortality.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Poxvirus infection should be considered in patients with febrile illness and vesiculopustular rash, especially in endemic areas or with animal contact. Clinical diagnosis is based on the characteristic rash and lymphadenopathy, though distinguishing it from chickenpox can be difficult early on. Suspected cases must be reported to health authorities. Laboratory diagnosis is necessary for confirmation, utilizing optimal clinical specimens such as scabs or swabs from vesicle bases, handled in Biosafety Level 2 facilities. Monkeypox virus can be identified by cell culture or PCR-based assays, including the Cepheid GeneXpert System for field diagnosis. Serologic assays are generally not sensitive enough for reliable diagnosis. The CDC developed specific case definitions, including clinical, epidemiologic, and laboratory criteria, for monkeypox.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment for monkeypox is primarily supportive. While data on the effectiveness of vaccinia immune globulin (VIG) for complications are limited, the CDC recommends considering it for prophylactic use in severely immunocompromised individuals exposed to monkeypox virus who cannot receive smallpox vaccination. Antivirals such as cidofovir and brincidofovir (CMX001) have shown in vitro and animal antiviral activity, with brincidofovir exhibiting greater potency and safety. The CDC recommends considering these for severe monkeypox cases. Tecovirimat (ST-246) has also demonstrated efficacy in animal studies but requires Investigational New Drug status for human use.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention in remote African regions is challenging due to limited healthcare access. Pre-exposure smallpox vaccination provided approximately 85% protection against monkeypox in past outbreaks, though prior vaccination did not provide complete protection in the US outbreak. While post-exposure vaccination efficacy is not fully known, extrapolation from smallpox suggests it may prevent or reduce disease severity if given within 3 days of exposure. The CDC recommends routine smallpox vaccination for laboratory personnel and healthcare/animal care personnel at risk of occupational exposure to Orthopoxviruses, provided they have no contraindications. Post-exposure vaccination decisions for individuals are made on a case-by-case basis in consultation with public health authorities.
